meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The real minimum wage is zero'?
meta.ogDescription: Thomas Sowell really wrote it, in a 2001 column on minimum-wage journalism. The popular one-liner trims his sentence, and the phrase itself was in use before him.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: Born 1930 · American economist, Hoover Institution senior fellow
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word in Sowell’s syndicated column “Minimum Journalism Evident in Wage Story” (Sun-Sentinel, 4 August 2001). He reprinted the column as “Minimum Journalism” in his collection Controversial Essays (2002). The popular one-liner cuts his sentence off at “zero.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Minimum Journalism Evident in Wage Story
As “Minimum Journalism” in Controversial Essays (Hoover Institution Press, 2002), pp. 48–49

source.excerpt: The minimum wage law is very cleverly misnamed. The real minimum wage is zero — and that is what many inexperienced and low-skilled people receive as a result of legislation that makes it illegal to pay them what they are currently worth to an employer.
trail: 28 September 1987: an opinion piece in Brigham Young University’s student paper, the Daily Universe, uses the identical sentence “The real minimum wage is zero.” and does not mention Sowell (scanned text at Internet Archive ↗).
4 August 2001: Sowell’s syndicated column, a critique of a Wall Street Journal front-page story on the minimum wage, contains the line (Sun-Sentinel ↗).
August 2001: the same column, credited to Thomas Sowell, is reposted online under the title “Anti-Capitalist Politically Correct Journalism at The Wall Street Journal” (Capitalism Magazine ↗).
2002: Sowell reprints the column as “Minimum Journalism” in Controversial Essays. Economist Don Boudreaux quotes the passage and cites it to pages 48–49 of that book (Cafe Hayek ↗).
source.excerptNote: In the popular version, Sowell’s sentence stops at “zero.” In the original, a dash carries it on to who pays that wage and why.

His long-running syndicated column and books such as Basic Economics made him a leading conservative voice on markets, and he received the National Humanities Medal in 2002.

misattribution.heading: What gets mixed up
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Sowell holds up. What gets muddled is the wording, a second, longer “zero” passage that people treat as the same quote, and the idea that Sowell coined the phrase.

items.why: “The real minimum wage is zero” is the opening of a longer sentence. Sowell goes on: “— and that is what many inexperienced and low-skilled people receive…” (Sun-Sentinel, 2001 ↗).

items.who: “Unfortunately, the real minimum wage is always zero, regardless of the laws…”
items.why: This is a separate, longer Sowell passage, and quote sites credit it to his book Basic Economics (Goodreads ↗). It is not the 2001 column sentence, so the two should not be cited as one quote.

BYU’s Daily Universe of 28 September 1987 printed the identical sentence with no reference to Sowell (Internet Archive ↗). Sowell wrote the line and made it famous, but this is no evidence that he invented the phrase.
The line is listed under “Unsourced” on the Talk page of Wikiquote’s Thomas Sowell entry, as “The real minimum wage is zero [unemployment].” (Wikiquote Talk ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Sowell did write the exact sentence, in his column of 4 August 2001 (Sun-Sentinel ↗). He reprinted it in Controversial Essays (2002).

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Sowell wrote the line in a column about journalism as much as economics. He objected that a Wall Street Journal front-page story on the minimum wage opened with an individual who, he argued, was “wholly atypical” of minimum-wage earners (Sun-Sentinel ↗).

His point was that a legal wage floor does not raise what an inexperienced worker is worth to an employer, so the worker who goes unhired is effectively paid nothing, and loses the experience a first job would bring. Many economists dispute how large that effect is in practice. Either way, the sentence became one of the most-quoted lines in the minimum-wage debate.
detailsBody: The pull-quote is from the same 2001 column, two sentences after the famous line. In full it reads: “But they cannot move up the ladder if they can’t get on the ladder.” (Capitalism Magazine reprint ↗).
